cse-2023-cs-35.approach: Decode P first: it is exactly $-16 = -2^4$. Multiplying by a power of two flips the sign and adds 4 to Q's biased exponent; Q's 23-bit fraction is copied unchanged.
concepts: Multiplying by a power of two

steps.title: Multiply sign, exponent and significand
steps.body:
- Sign: $1 \oplus 0 = 1$ (negative).
- Significand: $1.0 \times 1.f = 1.f$, already normalised, so the fraction is unchanged.
- Exponent: $2^4 \times 2^{-1} = 2^3$; biased $= 126 + 4 = 130 = 1000\,0010_2$.

$$P \times Q = -1.f \times 2^{3} \approx -13.76$$

optionAnalysis.reason: `0x404C2EF4` is positive (sign 0), has exponent 128 and a changed fraction ($100\,1100\ldots$). The product of a negative and a positive number is negative.
`0x405C2EF4` keeps the fraction but is positive with exponent 128, i.e. $+4Q$: wrong sign and wrong power of two.
Sign 1, exponent $126 + 4 = 130$, fraction of Q unchanged.
`0xC14C2EF4` has the right sign and exponent but the fraction starts $100\,1100$ instead of $101\,1100$; multiplying by $2^4$ never changes the fraction.

cse-2023-cs-35.shortcut: $\times(-16)$ means: add 4 to the exponent field, i.e. add $4 \times 2^{23} = \texttt{0x02000000}$, then set the sign bit: $\texttt{0x3F5C2EF4} + \texttt{0x02000000} = \texttt{0x415C2EF4}$, and with the sign bit set, $\texttt{0xC15C2EF4}$.
pitfalls: Adding the biased exponents ($131 + 126$) without subtracting the bias once.
Forgetting the sign: only options C and D are negative.
Reading the exponent from the first two hex digits: the exponent field straddles the nibble boundary (bits 30–23).
cse-2023-cs-35.verification: Decimal check: $1.f = 1 + \texttt{5C2EF4}/2^{23} = 1 + 6041332/8388608 \approx 1.7202$, so $Q \approx 0.8601$ and $P \times Q \approx -13.76$. Decoding C: $-1.7202 \times 2^{130-127} = -1.7202 \times 8 \approx -13.76$.

cse-2023-cs-36.approach: A max-heap is a complete binary tree of height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. EXTRACT-MAX sifts the moved last element down one root-to-leaf path and INSERT bubbles the new key up one leaf-to-root path, with $O(1)$ work per level.
concepts: Height of a complete binary tree

steps.title: Height of an n-element heap
steps.body:
A heap is a complete binary tree, so levels $0..h-1$ are full: $2^h \le n < 2^{h+1}$, which gives $h = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. Each operation below moves an element along one path, so it does at most $h$ swaps.

Example heap: $[50, 30, 40, 10, 20, 35, 25]$, $n = 7$, $h = \lfloor \log_2 7 \rfloor = 2$.

scene.caption: $n = 7$, height $2$

steps.title: EXTRACT-MAX: sift-down, O(log n)
steps.body:
Reading the maximum (the root) is $O(1)$, but it must also be **deleted**: move the last element to the root, shrink the heap, and sift down. At each level compare with both children and swap with the larger one. That is at most $h$ swaps.

In the example: remove 50, move 25 to the root; $25 < 40$ swap; $25 < 35$ swap. That is 2 swaps $= h$, the worst case.

scene.caption: After EXTRACT-MAX: 25 sank 2 levels

steps.title: INSERT: sift-up, O(log n)
steps.body:
Put the key in the next free leaf and swap it with its parent while it is larger. That is at most $h$ swaps; the worst case is a key larger than everything, which rises to the root.

In the example: insert 45 as the right child of 35; $45 > 35$ swap; $45 > 40$ swap. Two swaps $= h$.

scene.caption: After INSERT(45): 45 rose 2 levels

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both operations are $O(\log n)$ in the worst case, option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: Neither is $O(1)$ in the worst case: both may move an element through all $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ levels.
Each operation walks one root-leaf path of a tree of height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
EXTRACT-MAX must restore the heap ($O(\log n)$), and INSERT never needs $O(n)$: it only compares along one path.
Confuses EXTRACT-MAX with FIND-MAX (peek), which is $O(1)$; deleting the root needs a sift-down.

cse-2023-cs-36.shortcut: Only FIND-MAX is $O(1)$ in a binary heap; every operation that changes the heap (insert, delete, extract, increase-key) is $O(\log n)$.
pitfalls: Confusing *extract* (read and delete) with *peek*.
Quoting $O(n)$ for insert: $O(n)$ is BUILD-HEAP or searching for an arbitrary key, not insertion.
Using the average case (insert of a random key is $O(1)$ expected); the question asks for the worst case.
cse-2023-cs-36.verification: In the 7-element example both operations took exactly $2 = \lfloor \log_2 7 \rfloor$ swaps, and each swap moves the element one level, so no operation can exceed the height.

cse-2023-cs-37.approach: `foo` returns the sum of a subtree and prints it **after** both recursive calls, so it prints subtree sums in post-order. List the nodes in post-order and write each subtree sum.

steps.title: What foo prints, and when
steps.body:
`foo(NULL)` $= 0$, and otherwise `retval = val + foo(left) + foo(right)`, which is the sum of the subtree. The `printf` runs after both recursive calls, so the order is **left, right, node** (post-order).

Post-order of the tree: $3, 8, 5, 13, 11, 10$.

scene.caption: Print order = post-order

steps.title: Right subtree of 10
steps.body:
`foo(11)` first calls `foo(NULL)` $= 0$ (prints nothing), then

- `foo(13)` $= 13$, prints **13**
- `foo(11)` $= 11 + 0 + 13 = 24$, prints **24**

optionAnalysis.reason: Plain post-order of the node **values**; `foo` prints subtree sums, not `p->val`.
In-order of the values (sorted, since the tree is a BST); neither the order nor the values match.
Subtree sums in post-order: $3, 8, 16, 13, 24, 50$.
The right sums but in in-order (3, 16, 8, 50, 24, 13); the print happens after both calls, not between them.

cse-2023-cs-37.shortcut: The last number printed is the root's subtree sum, i.e. the sum of all nodes: $10 + 5 + 11 + 3 + 8 + 13 = 50$. Only C ends in 50, since D prints 50 in the middle.
pitfalls: Printing `p->val` instead of `retval`.
Placing the print between the calls (in-order) or before them (pre-order).
cse-2023-cs-37.verification: Every leaf prints its own value (3, 8, 13), each internal node prints its value plus its children's sums ($5+3+8=16$, $11+0+13=24$), and the root prints the grand total 50.

cse-2023-cs-38.approach: Build a separating permutation in independent stages and multiply (product rule): choose the $2k$ positions holding $A \cup B$, arrange the other $n - 2k$ elements, decide which set comes first, and order each set inside its block.

steps.title: Positions of A ∪ B
steps.body: Choose which $2k$ of the $n$ positions hold the elements of $A \cup B$: $\binom{n}{2k}$ ways. In a separating permutation the first $k$ of these positions hold one set and the last $k$ hold the other.

steps.title: The other n − 2k elements
steps.body: The remaining $n - 2k$ elements fill the remaining positions in any order: $(n - 2k)!$ ways.

steps.title: Which set goes first
steps.body: Either all of $A$ precedes all of $B$, or all of $B$ precedes all of $A$: 2 ways. Since $k \ge 1$, both cannot hold at once, so the two cases do not overlap.

steps.title: Order inside each block
steps.body: The $k$ elements of $A$ can be ordered in $k!$ ways within their block, and likewise $k!$ for $B$: $(k!)^2$.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body:
$$\binom{n}{2k}\,(n-2k)! \times 2 \times (k!)^2 = 2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!\,(k!)^2$$

which is option (D).

optionAnalysis.reason: $n!$ counts every permutation; for $k \ge 2$ many do not separate, e.g. $a_1 b_1 a_2 b_2 \ldots$.
Places the other elements but forgets the internal orders $(k!)^2$ of $A$ and $B$ and the factor 2.
Counts only the case "$A$ before $B$"; the factor 2 for "$B$ before $A$" is missing.
Positions $\binom{n}{2k}$, others $(n-2k)!$, which set first $2$, internal orders $(k!)^2$.

cse-2023-cs-38.shortcut: Symmetry: the relative order of the $2k$ elements of $A \cup B$ is uniform over $(2k)!$ orders, of which $2(k!)^2$ separate. Count $= n! \cdot \frac{2(k!)^2}{(2k)!} = 2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!\,(k!)^2$, since $\frac{n!}{(2k)!} = \binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!$.
pitfalls: Reading "one of the following is true" as only the first bullet (losing the factor 2).
Forgetting that the elements inside $A$ (and inside $B$) can be permuted.
cse-2023-cs-38.verification: Small case $n = 4$, $k = 2$, $A = \{1,2\}$, $B = \{3,4\}$: separating permutations are $12\,34$, $21\,34$, $12\,43$, $21\,43$ and the 4 with $B$ first, giving 8. Formula: $2 \cdot \binom{4}{4} \cdot 0! \cdot (2!)^2 = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 4 = 8$.

cse-2023-cs-39.approach: Check each property straight from the definition of $\sim$: equal classes force equal $f$-values (well-defined), $f$ onto gives $F$ onto, and equal $F$-values force equal classes (one-to-one).

steps.title: F is well-defined
steps.body: A class can be named by any of its members, so $F$ must not depend on the representative. If $[x] = [y]$ then $x \sim y$, i.e. $f(x) = f(y)$, so $F([x]) = f(x) = f(y) = F([y])$. Hence $F$ is well-defined and **(A) is false**.

scene.caption: Example: 1 and 2 share the image p, so they form one class.

steps.title: F is onto
steps.body: Take any $b \in B$. Since $f$ is onto, some $a \in A$ has $f(a) = b$, and then $F([a]) = f(a) = b$. So **(B) is true**.

scene.caption: Every element of B is hit.

steps.title: F is one-to-one
steps.body: Suppose $F([x]) = F([y])$. Then $f(x) = f(y)$, which by definition means $x \sim y$, so $[x] = [y]$. So **(C) is true**, even though $f$ itself need not be one-to-one.

scene.caption: Distinct classes have distinct images.

steps.title: Bijective
steps.body: One-to-one and onto, so $F$ is a bijection $\mathcal{E} \to B$: **(D) is true**. Answer: **B, C, D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $F$ is well-defined: members of one class have the same $f$-value by the very definition of $\sim$.
Every $b \in B$ equals $f(a)$ for some $a$, hence equals $F([a])$.
$F([x]) = F([y]) \Rightarrow f(x) = f(y) \Rightarrow x \sim y \Rightarrow [x] = [y]$.
Onto (B) and one-to-one (C) together make $F$ a bijection.

cse-2023-cs-39.shortcut: Grouping $A$ into the fibres $f^{-1}(b)$ of a surjection gives exactly one class per $b \in B$, so $\lvert \mathcal{E} \rvert = \lvert B \rvert$ and $F$ matches them one to one.
pitfalls: Thinking $F$ inherits the non-injectivity of $f$: collapsing each fibre to one class removes it.
Ticking A because $F$ is defined via a representative; it is well-defined precisely because $\sim$ is defined by $f$.
cse-2023-cs-39.verification: Example $f$: $1, 2 \mapsto p$, $3 \mapsto q$, $4, 5 \mapsto r$. Classes $\{1,2\}, \{3\}, \{4,5\}$ map to $p, q, r$: three classes, three images, each hit once.

cse-2023-cs-40.approach: A byte-stream protocol numbers bytes, and a sequence number must not be reused while an old segment carrying it can still be alive, i.e. within one maximum segment lifetime. So $2^{n}$ must be at least the number of bytes that can be sent in one MSL.
cse-2023-cs-40.given: Bandwidth $100$ Mbps, RTT $150$ ms, MSL $= 2$ min $= 120$ s. Sequence numbers count bytes.

steps.title: Bytes that can be sent in one MSL
steps.body:
$$100 \text{ Mbps} = \frac{100 \times 10^6}{8} = 1.25 \times 10^7 \text{ bytes/s}$$

$$1.25 \times 10^7 \times 120 = 1.5 \times 10^9 \text{ bytes}$$

All of these need distinct sequence numbers.

steps.title: Check each option by wrap-around time
steps.body:
Wrap time $= 2^n / (1.25 \times 10^7)$ s, which must be at least $120$ s:

| Bits | $2^n$ | Wrap time | Valid? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | $1\,073\,741\,824$ | $\approx 85.9$ s | no |
| 32 | $4\,294\,967\,296$ | $\approx 343.6$ s | yes |
| 34 | $17\,179\,869\,184$ | $\approx 1374.4$ s | yes |
| 36 | $68\,719\,476\,736$ | $\approx 5497.6$ s | yes |

The RTT (150 ms) does not matter here; it sizes the window (bandwidth × RTT), not the sequence space. Answer: **B, C, D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^{30}$ bytes are sent in about 85.9 s < 120 s MSL, so numbers would wrap while old duplicates may still be alive.
$2^{32}$ bytes take about 343.6 s ≥ 120 s to wrap.
$2^{34}$ bytes take about 1374 s to wrap, comfortably above the MSL.
$2^{36}$ bytes take about 5498 s to wrap; longer fields are always safe.

cse-2023-cs-40.shortcut: $\log_2(1.5 \times 10^9) = \log_2 1.5 + 9\log_2 10 \approx 0.585 + 29.9 = 30.48$, so at least 31 bits; every option from 32 bits up works.
pitfalls: Counting bits instead of bytes ($10^8 \times 120 = 1.2 \times 10^{10}$ would demand 34 bits and wrongly reject 32).
Using the RTT in place of the MSL: wrap-around safety is about how long old segments survive, not the RTT.
Counting segments instead of bytes: in a byte stream every byte gets a number.
cse-2023-cs-40.verification: Real TCP uses 32-bit byte sequence numbers; at 100 Mbps that is safe for about 343 s, more than the 120 s MSL, consistent with 32 bits being valid and 30 bits not.

cse-2023-cs-41.approach: Check the group axioms for symmetric difference: closure, associativity (Δ is XOR of membership), identity $\emptyset$, and inverses, where $A \Delta A = \emptyset$ makes every set its own inverse.

steps.title: Closure and associativity
steps.body:
$A \Delta B \subseteq X$, so it is again in $2^X$ (closure).

An element $x$ is in $A \Delta B$ iff it lies in **exactly one** of $A, B$, i.e. its membership bits XOR to 1. XOR is associative, so $(A \Delta B) \Delta C$ and $A \Delta (B \Delta C)$ are both the set of elements lying in an odd number of $A, B, C$. So $\Delta$ is associative.

steps.title: Identity: the empty set
steps.body:
$$A \Delta \emptyset = (A - \emptyset) \cup (\emptyset - A) = A \cup \emptyset = A$$

and $\emptyset \Delta A = A$ likewise, so $e = \emptyset$.

steps.title: Inverse: every set is its own
steps.body:
$$A \Delta A = (A - A) \cup (A - A) = \emptyset = e$$

so $A^{-1} = A$: **(D) is true**. The complement does not work: $A \Delta \overline{A} = A \cup \overline{A} = X \neq \emptyset$ whenever $X$ is nonempty, so **(C) is false**.

scene.caption: Diagonal is all ∅: each set is its own inverse.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Closure, associativity, identity and inverses all hold, so $H$ is a group (indeed abelian, since $\Delta$ is symmetric): **(A) is true**, which makes **(B) false**. Answer: **A, D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\Delta$ is closed and associative, $\emptyset$ is the identity, and every element has an inverse.
Its first half is true, but $H$ *is* a group, so the statement is false.
$A \Delta \overline{A} = X$, not the identity $\emptyset$ (for nonempty $X$). The complement would be the inverse only if $X$ were the identity.
$A \Delta A = \emptyset$, the identity.

cse-2023-cs-41.shortcut: Identify each subset with its characteristic bit-vector: $\Delta$ becomes bitwise XOR on $\{0,1\}^{\lvert X \rvert}$, a group in which $0$ is the identity and every vector is its own inverse.
pitfalls: Taking $X$ as the identity (that is the identity for $\cap$, not $\Delta$), which leads to option C.
Doubting associativity because $\Delta$ is defined with set differences; the XOR view settles it.
cse-2023-cs-41.verification: For $X = \{1, 2\}$ the Cayley table of $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1,2\}\}$ is a Latin square with $\emptyset$ on the diagonal: the Klein four-group.

cse-2023-cs-42.approach: Add three delays: iterative DNS (one RTT per tier: root, TLD, authoritative), then the TCP handshake plus the HTML request, then the 10 objects. Non-persistent connections cost 2 RTT per batch of 5 objects; one persistent pipelined connection fetches all 10 in 1 RTT.
cse-2023-cs-42.given: DNS: 3 tiers, iterative, nothing cached, RTT to each server. Web server RTT also 1 RTT. HTML + 10 small objects (transmission time negligible).

steps.title: DNS: 3 RTT
steps.body: The local DNS server is on the local host and works iteratively: query root (1 RTT) → referral to the TLD server (1 RTT) → referral to the authoritative server (1 RTT), which returns the IP address. Total **3 RTT**.

steps.title: Base HTML file: 2 RTT
steps.body: TCP handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK takes **1 RTT**; the final ACK carries the HTTP GET, and the HTML comes back after **1 RTT**. Elapsed so far: $3 + 2 = 5$ RTT.

steps.title: Non-persistent HTTP, 5 parallel connections
steps.body:
Every object needs its own TCP connection: handshake (1 RTT) + request/response (1 RTT) $= 2$ RTT per batch. With 5 in parallel, the 10 objects need $10 / 5 = 2$ batches, so $2 \times 2 = 4$ RTT.

$$3 + 2 + 4 = 9 \text{ RTT}$$

So **(C) is correct** and (A) is not.

scene.caption: Non-persistent: done at 9 RTT.

steps.title: Persistent HTTP with pipelining
steps.body:
The connection used for the HTML stays open. The browser sends all 10 GETs back-to-back and the 10 small objects return within **1 RTT**:

$$3 + 2 + 1 = 6 \text{ RTT}$$

So **(D) is correct** and (B) is not. Answer: **C, D**.

scene.title: Persistent HTTP with pipelining
scene.caption: Persistent + pipelining: done at 6 RTT.

answer.value: **C, D** (9 RTT non-persistent with 5 parallel connections; 6 RTT persistent with pipelining)

optionAnalysis.reason: 7 RTT counts only 1 RTT per object batch, forgetting that non-persistent HTTP opens a new TCP connection (one more RTT) for every object.
5 RTT is the time to get just the HTML (3 DNS + 2); the pipelined objects still need 1 more RTT.
$3$ (DNS) $+ 2$ (HTML) $+ 2 \times 2$ (two batches of 5 non-persistent fetches) $= 9$ RTT.
$3$ (DNS) $+ 2$ (HTML) $+ 1$ (all 10 objects pipelined) $= 6$ RTT.

cse-2023-cs-42.shortcut: Common part = 3 (DNS) + 2 (HTML) = 5 RTT. Then add $2\lceil 10/5 \rceil = 4$ for non-persistent parallel, or $1$ for persistent pipelined.
pitfalls: Counting DNS as 1 RTT: an iterative lookup over 3 tiers with empty caches needs 3 round trips.
Forgetting the TCP handshake before the first GET.
Reusing connections in the non-persistent case: each object needs a fresh handshake.
cse-2023-cs-42.verification: The two answers differ by exactly the object phase: non-persistent spends $4$ RTT (2 batches × 2) where pipelined spends $1$, and $9 - 6 = 4 - 1 = 3$.

cse-2023-cs-43.approach: Write the 4 equally likely outcomes, list each event as a set of outcomes, and test independence with the definition $P(X\cap Y)=P(X)\,P(Y)$. With only 4 outcomes, counting is faster and safer than intuition.
cse-2023-cs-43.given: Two fair coins. $A$ = HEAD on both throws, $B$ = HEAD on the 1st throw, $C$ = HEAD on the 2nd throw.

steps.title: Sample space and the three events
steps.body:
$\Omega=\{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$, each with probability $\tfrac14$.

| Event | Outcomes | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ | $\{HH\}$ | $\tfrac14$ |
| $B$ | $\{HH, HT\}$ | $\tfrac24=\tfrac12$ |
| $C$ | $\{HH, TH\}$ | $\tfrac24=\tfrac12$ |

steps.title: A and B: not independent
steps.body:
$A\cap B=\{HH\}$, so $P(A\cap B)=\tfrac14$.

But $P(A)\,P(B)=\tfrac14\times\tfrac12=\tfrac18$.

Since $\tfrac14\neq\tfrac18$, $A$ and $B$ are **dependent** — knowing $B$ happened doubles the chance of $A$ ($P(A\mid B)=\tfrac{1/4}{1/2}=\tfrac12$). By the same symmetry $A\cap C=\{HH\}$ and $P(A)P(C)=\tfrac18\neq\tfrac14$, so $A$ and $C$ are dependent too.

steps.title: B and C: independent
steps.body:
$B\cap C=\{HH\}$, so $P(B\cap C)=\tfrac14$, and $P(B)\,P(C)=\tfrac12\times\tfrac12=\tfrac14$.

Equal, so $B$ and $C$ **are independent** (the two tosses do not influence each other).

steps.title: Conditional probability P(B | C)
steps.body:
$$P(B\mid C)=\frac{P(B\cap C)}{P(C)}=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac12=P(B).$$

So statement (D) is true — it is just a restatement of the independence of $B$ and $C$ (valid because $P(C)>0$).

answer.value: **(C) and (D)** — $B$ and $C$ are independent and $P(B\mid C)=P(B)=\tfrac12$

optionAnalysis.reason: $P(A\cap B)=\tfrac14$ but $P(A)P(B)=\tfrac18$. $A\subset B$, so $B$ occurring makes $A$ more likely — the classic dependent pair.
Same as (A) by symmetry: $A\subset C$, $P(A\cap C)=\tfrac14\neq\tfrac18$.
$P(B\cap C)=P(HH)=\tfrac14=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=P(B)P(C)$.
$P(B\mid C)=\tfrac{1/4}{1/2}=\tfrac12=P(B)$; equivalent to (C) since $P(C)\neq0$.

cse-2023-cs-43.shortcut: Events about **different** fair tosses ($B$, $C$) are independent, so (C) and (D) hold together. An event that contains another non-trivial event ($A\subset B$ with $0<P(A)<P(B)<1$) is never independent of it, because $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\neq P(A)P(B)$.
pitfalls: Confusing *independent* with *mutually exclusive*: $B$ and $C$ overlap (both contain $HH$) yet are independent.
Picking only (C): (D) is the same fact written as a conditional probability, so the two always stand or fall together here.
cse-2023-cs-43.verification: Check (C) via complements: $P(\bar B\cap\bar C)=P(TT)=\tfrac14=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=P(\bar B)P(\bar C)$, consistent with independence. For (A): $P(A\mid B)=\tfrac12\neq P(A)=\tfrac14$.

cse-2023-cs-44.approach: Count the executions exactly as a sum: Function_1 does $n + \lfloor n/2\rfloor + \lfloor n/4\rfloor + \dots$ (a geometric series, between $n$ and $2n$), Function_2 does exactly $100n$. Both are linear, so compare growth rates directly.

steps.title: Count f₂(n)
steps.body: The single loop runs for $i=1$ to $100n$, so $f_2(n)=100n$, i.e. $f_2(n)\in\Theta(n)$.

steps.title: Count f₁(n): one pass per halving
steps.body:
Each pass of the while loop runs the for loop $n$ times for the **current** $n$, then halves $n$. The loop stops when $n\le1$, so

$$f_1(n)=n+\left\lfloor\tfrac n2\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\tfrac n4\right\rfloor+\dots\quad(\text{terms}>1).$$

For $n=16$: $16+8+4+2=30$ (the next value is $1$, which fails $n>1$).

steps.title: Bound f₁(n) between n and 2n
steps.body:
Lower bound (for $n\ge2$): the first pass alone gives $f_1(n)\ge n$.

Upper bound: $f_1(n)\le n\left(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\dots\right)<n\cdot\frac{1}{1-\tfrac12}=2n$.

So $n\le f_1(n)<2n$, i.e. $f_1(n)\in\Theta(n)$ — in particular $f_1(n)\in O(n)$.

steps.title: Compare f₁ with f₂
steps.body:
$$\frac{n}{100n}\le\frac{f_1(n)}{f_2(n)}<\frac{2n}{100n}\;\Longrightarrow\;\frac{1}{100}\le\frac{f_1(n)}{f_2(n)}<\frac{1}{50}.$$

The ratio stays between two positive constants, so $f_1(n)\in\Theta(f_2(n))$. It does **not** tend to $0$ (rules out $o$) and does **not** tend to $\infty$ (rules out $\omega$).

optionAnalysis.reason: $f_1(n)=\Theta(n)$ and $f_2(n)=100n=\Theta(n)$; the ratio lies in $[\tfrac1{100},\tfrac1{50})$.
$o$ needs $f_1/f_2\to0$. The ratio never drops below $\tfrac1{100}$ — the constant 100 does not change the growth rate.
$\omega$ needs $f_1/f_2\to\infty$. Those who treat the nested loops as $n\log n$ (n work for each of $\log n$ passes) pick this, but each pass does only half the previous work.

cse-2023-cs-44.shortcut: "Halve the work each round" ⇒ total $\le 2\times$ the first round. So Function_1 is linear; Function_2 is linear; constants never matter in $\Theta$.
pitfalls: Multiplying loop bounds blindly: $n$ iterations $\times\ \log n$ passes $= n\log n$ is only an upper bound, not tight.
Thinking the factor 100 makes $f_1\in o(f_2)$ — constant factors are absorbed by $\Theta$.
cse-2023-cs-44.verification: $n=1024$: $f_1=1024+512+\dots+2=2046<2048=2n$, and $f_2=102400$; ratio $\approx0.02$, between $\tfrac1{100}$ and $\tfrac1{50}$ as predicted.

cse-2023-cs-45.approach: Prove the two general facts directly from the rule (a vertex never takes a neighbour's colour; at most $\Delta$ colours are blocked), then kill the other two statements with one small counterexample: a 4-vertex path coloured in a bad order.

steps.title: Statement A: the colouring is always proper
steps.body: When $v_i$ is coloured, it takes a colour $j$ that **no already-coloured neighbour** has. Take any edge $v_av_b$ with $a<b$: $v_a$ is coloured first, so when $v_b$ is coloured, colour$(v_a)$ is forbidden for it. Hence the two ends of every edge differ — the colouring is proper.

steps.title: Statement B: at most Δ(G) + 1 colours
steps.body: $v_i$ has at most $\Delta(G)$ neighbours, so at most $\Delta(G)$ distinct colours are blocked. Among the $\Delta(G)+1$ colours $\{1,\dots,\Delta(G)+1\}$ at least one is free, so the minimum free colour is $\le\Delta(G)+1$. This holds for every vertex, so the whole colouring uses at most $\Delta(G)+1$ colours.

steps.title: Counterexample: path coloured in a bad order
steps.body:
Take the path $v_1 - v_3 - v_4 - v_2$ (edges $v_1v_3$, $v_3v_4$, $v_4v_2$), so $\Delta=2$. Greedy colours in index order:

- $v_1$: no coloured neighbour → colour **1**.
- $v_2$: its only neighbour $v_4$ is uncoloured → colour **1**.

steps.title: Greedy is forced to a third colour
steps.body:
- $v_3$: neighbours $v_1$ (1) and $v_4$ (uncoloured) → smallest free colour **2**.
- $v_4$: neighbours $v_3$ (2) and $v_2$ (1) → colours 1 and 2 are blocked → colour **3**.

Greedy used $3$ colours.

steps.title: Statements C and D fail
steps.body:
- **C** is false: $3>\Delta=2$ colours were used. (Any complete graph $K_n$ also shows it: greedy needs $n=\Delta+1$ colours.)
- **D** is false: a path is bipartite, so its chromatic number is $2$ (colour $v_1,v_4$ with 1 and $v_3,v_2$ with 2), yet greedy used $3$.

So only **A** and **B** are always true.

scene.caption: Greedy used 3 colours; χ(path) = 2 and Δ = 2

answer.value: **(A) and (B)** — always a proper colouring, with at most $\Delta(G)+1$ colours

optionAnalysis.reason: Every vertex avoids the colours of its already-coloured neighbours, so no edge gets equal colours at its ends.
At most $\Delta$ colours are blocked for any vertex, so a colour $\le\Delta+1$ is always free.
$K_{\Delta+1}$ (or the badly ordered path, $\Delta=2$, 3 colours) needs $\Delta+1$ colours. $\Delta$ colours suffice only in special cases (Brooks' theorem), not for greedy in general.
Greedy depends on the vertex order; on the path $v_1v_3v_4v_2$ it uses 3 colours while $\chi=2$. Computing $\chi$ is NP-hard, so no simple greedy rule can guarantee it.

cse-2023-cs-45.shortcut: Remember: greedy colouring is always **proper** and uses $\le\Delta+1$ colours; it is **not** optimal (order-dependent) and can **not** promise $\le\Delta$ ($K_n$ needs $n=\Delta+1$).
pitfalls: Believing greedy is optimal: it is optimal for *some* order, but the question fixes the order $v_1,\dots,v_n$ arbitrarily.
Mixing up Brooks' theorem ($\chi\le\Delta$ except complete graphs and odd cycles) with what greedy achieves.
cse-2023-cs-45.verification: $K_3$: $\Delta=2$, greedy colours 1, 2, 3 → 3 colours $=\Delta+1$, consistent with B and contradicting C; the path example contradicts D while still obeying A and B.

cse-2023-cs-46.approach: Look at the start vertex's neighbourhood: $\emptyset$ is a proper subset of every non-empty set, so it is adjacent to **all** other 7 vertices. BFS therefore discovers everything in its first round, in any order — count the permutations.
cse-2023-cs-46.given: $V=2^U$ with $U=\{1,2,3\}$ (8 vertices); $A\sim B \iff A\subsetneq B$ or $B\subsetneq A$. Count the BFS orders from $\emptyset$.

steps.title: The graph: comparable subsets are adjacent
steps.body: There are $2^3=8$ vertices. Two different subsets are adjacent exactly when one strictly contains the other. In total there are $3^3-2^3=27-8=19$ such pairs (dashed edges are the 12 that do not involve $\emptyset$).

steps.title: Neighbours of ∅: everything else
steps.body: $\emptyset\subsetneq X$ for every non-empty $X$, so $\emptyset$ is adjacent to all $8-1=7$ other vertices: $\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{1,2,3\}$.

steps.title: BFS from ∅ visits all 7 in one round
steps.body:
BFS visits $\emptyset$, then dequeues it and visits all its unvisited neighbours. The adjacency order is not fixed, so **any** of the $7!$ orders of these neighbours is a valid BFS order. After this round every vertex is visited, so the rest of the search adds nothing and cannot change the order.

One example (badge = visit position): $\emptyset,\{2,3\},\{1\},\{1,2,3\},\{3\},\{1,2\},\{2\},\{1,3\}$.

steps.title: Count the orderings
steps.body:
The first vertex is fixed ($\emptyset$); the other 7 may come in any order:

$$\lvert\mathcal{B}(\emptyset)\rvert = 7! = 7\times6\times5\times4\times3\times2\times1 = 5040.$$

cse-2023-cs-46.shortcut: If the BFS source is adjacent to every other vertex of an $n$-vertex graph, the number of BFS orders is $(n-1)!$. Here $n=8$: $7!=5040$.
pitfalls: Treating the graph as the Hasse diagram (only "cover" edges such as $\emptyset$–$\{1\}$, a 3-cube): BFS would then go level by level and the count would be far smaller. The edge rule here is *any* proper containment, so $\emptyset$–$\{1,2,3\}$ is an edge too.
Counting only the orders of the singletons, or forgetting that $\{1,2,3\}$ is also adjacent to $\emptyset$.
cse-2023-cs-46.verification: Contrast with a start vertex like $\{1\}$: its neighbours are $\emptyset,\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{1,2,3\}$ only, so the count there would be different and smaller — the special thing about $\emptyset$ is degree $7=n-1$.

cse-2023-cs-47.approach: Map rows to pages (4 rows per page → 32 pages), notice the inner loop walks **down a column**, touching all 32 pages once per column. With only 30 frames, LRU on a cyclic scan of 32 pages evicts each page just before it is needed again, so every page faults in every column.
cse-2023-cs-47.given: int D[128][128] (row-major), 512 elements per frame, 30 frames, LRU; loop order: outer $i$ (column), inner $j$ (row), access $D[j][i]$.

steps.title: Which page holds D[j][i]?
steps.body: One row has $128$ elements, a page holds $512=4\times128$ elements, so **one page = 4 consecutive rows**. The array has $\frac{128\times128}{512}=\frac{16384}{512}=32$ pages, and $D[j][i]$ is in page $P_{\lfloor j/4\rfloor}$ (independent of $i$).

scene.caption: $D[j][i]$ lies in page $P_{\lfloor j/4\rfloor}$: P0 = rows 0–3, …, P31 = rows 124–127

steps.title: Column i = 0: 32 faults
steps.body:
For fixed $i$, $j=0\dots127$ touches $P_0,P_0,P_0,P_0,P_1,\dots,P_{31}$: each page 4 times in a row. The first touch faults, the next 3 hit (the page was just used).

$P_0\dots P_{29}$ fill the 30 frames (30 faults). $P_{30}$ evicts the LRU page $P_0$ and $P_{31}$ evicts $P_1$: **32 faults**. Resident now: $P_2\dots P_{31}$.

scene.caption: After column 0: P2 … P31 resident (30 frames), P0 and P1 evicted

steps.title: Column i = 1: every page is missing again
steps.body:
The scan restarts at $P_0$ — not resident → fault, evicting the LRU page $P_2$. Then $P_1$ faults and evicts $P_3$; $P_2$ faults and evicts $P_4$; … each page is evicted two steps before it is needed. So column 1 again costs **32 faults**, and after $P_{31}$ the frames again hold $P_2\dots P_{31}$.

This repeats identically for every column.

scene.caption: Column 1, after $j=0\dots7$: P0, P1 re-faulted and evicted P2, P3

steps.title: Total over 128 columns
steps.body: $$\text{faults}=128\ \text{columns}\times32\ \text{faults per column}=4096.$$

scene.caption: Every column faults on all 32 pages

cse-2023-cs-47.shortcut: Pages touched per column $=32>30$ frames, and the scan is cyclic, so LRU thrashes: faults $=$ (columns) $\times$ (pages per column) $=128\times32$.
pitfalls: Counting 128 faults per column (one per element): the 4 rows of a page are consecutive in $j$, so only the first of them faults.
Answering 32 (as if the array fit in memory): it needs 32 frames but only 30 are allocated.
Thinking only 2 pages per column fault after the first column — with LRU and a cyclic scan longer than the frame count, *every* reference to a new page misses.
cse-2023-cs-47.verification: Row-wise order ($D[i][j]$) would fault only $32$ times (each page loaded once). Column-wise with $\ge32$ frames would also give $32$. With $30<32$ frames LRU's worst case for cyclic scans appears: $32\times128=4096$.

cse-2023-cs-48.approach: Each page-table page is one 4 KB page, so it holds $4096/8=512=2^9$ entries and translates 9 bits of the virtual page number. Divide the VPN bits by 9.
cse-2023-cs-48.given: VA = 57 bits, page = 4 KB = $2^{12}$ B, PTE = 8 B at every level, each page-table node fits in one page.

steps.title: Offset and VPN bits
steps.body:
Page size $4\text{ KB}=2^{12}$ B → page offset $=12$ bits.

VPN bits $=57-12=45$.

steps.title: Bits resolved per level
steps.body: A page-table page is one page of $2^{12}$ B and an entry is $8=2^3$ B, so it holds $\frac{2^{12}}{2^3}=2^9=512$ entries — indexed by **9 bits**.

steps.title: Number of levels
steps.body:
$$L=\left\lceil\frac{45}{9}\right\rceil=5.$$

$45=5\times9$ exactly, so every level (including the top) is a full 512-entry page.

cse-2023-cs-48.shortcut: Bits per level $=\log_2(\text{page}/\text{PTE})=12-3=9$; $L=\lceil(57-12)/9\rceil=5$. (This is exactly Intel's 5-level paging for 57-bit addresses.)
pitfalls: Forgetting to remove the 12 offset bits: $\lceil57/9\rceil=7$ is wrong.
Using $4096/4$ entries (4-byte PTE) instead of $4096/8$: the PTE is 8 bytes here.
cse-2023-cs-48.verification: Reverse check: $5$ levels $\times\ 9$ bits $+\ 12$ offset bits $=45+12=57$ bits. With 4 levels only $4\times9+12=48$ bits could be translated — the familiar x86-64 4-level case.

cse-2023-cs-49.approach: Simulate both structures operation by operation, tracking stack top and queue front. "Repeat operation VII three times" means VII runs three **more** times, moving the queue's remaining elements onto the stack.

steps.title: III, IV: pop and dequeue
steps.body:
III: pop $S$ → removes $2$; $S=[1,5,7,8,9]$.

IV: dequeue $Q$ → removes $1$; $Q=[5,7,8,9,2]$.

steps.title: V, VI: pop and dequeue again
steps.body:
V: pop → removes $9$; $S=[1,5,7,8]$.

VI: dequeue → removes $5$; $Q=[7,8,9,2]$.

steps.title: VII: move the front of Q onto S
VIII: repeat VII three times
steps.body:
Move $8$, then $9$, then $2$:

$S=[1,5,7,8,7,8,9,2]$ (top $=2$), $Q=[\,]$ — exactly the 3 remaining elements, so the queue is empty but no dequeue fails.

steps.title: IX, X: two pops
steps.body:
IX: pop → removes $2$. X: pop → removes $9$.

$S=[1,5,7,8,7,8]$, so the **top is 8**.

cse-2023-cs-49.shortcut: After VI, $Q=[7,8,9,2]$ and $S=[1,5,7,8]$. VII+VIII push all four in queue order, so $S=[1,5,7,8,\,7,8,9,2]$; two pops remove $2,9$ → top $=8$.
pitfalls: Running VII only three times in total (VII + 2 repeats): $S=[\dots,7,8,9]$, two pops leave top $=7$. "Repeat VII three times" adds three executions after VII.
Popping from the wrong end: the stack removes the most recent push ($2$, then $9$), the queue removes the oldest ($1$, then $5$).
cse-2023-cs-49.verification: Element count: $S$ has $6-2+4-2=6$ elements and $Q$ has $6-2-4=0$ — consistent with the final $S=[1,5,7,8,7,8]$.

cse-2023-cs-50.approach: Build the parse tree of $10\#011$ and evaluate the synthesized attributes bottom-up. Recognise the meaning: $I$ reads the bits before # as a binary integer, $F$ reads the bits after # as a binary fraction, so the result is $10.011_2$.

steps.title: Parse tree of 10#011
steps.body:
$N\to I\,\#\,F$.

- $I$ derives "10": $I\to I_1B$, with $I_1\to B\to\mathbf 1$ and $B\to\mathbf 0$.
- $F$ derives "011": $F\to B\,F_1$ with $B\to\mathbf 0$; $F_1\to B\,F_2$ with $B\to\mathbf 1$; $F_2\to B\to\mathbf 1$.

steps.title: Integer part: I.val = 2
steps.body:
Leaves: $B.val$ = token value.

$I_1.val=B.val=1$.

$I.val=2\cdot I_1.val+B.val=2\cdot1+0=2$ (binary $10_2=2$).

cse-2023-cs-50.shortcut: The scheme converts a binary number "integer#fraction" to decimal: $10.011_2=2+\tfrac14+\tfrac18=2.375$.
pitfalls: Evaluating $F$ left-to-right like $I$: $F$ is right-recursive, so the innermost (rightmost) bit is halved most — each step is $\tfrac12(\text{bit}+\text{rest})$.
Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ in $F\to B$, which would give $F=0.75$ and $N=2.75$.
cse-2023-cs-50.verification: Unrolling $F$: $\tfrac12\big(0+\tfrac12(1+\tfrac12\cdot1)\big)=\tfrac{0}{2}+\tfrac14+\tfrac18=0.375$, i.e. the binary fraction $.011$. Total $2.375$.

cse-2023-cs-51.approach: A WHERE clause with AND keeps a row only if **both** conditions are true. Test each of the 5 rows; watch the strict inequality $> 65$.

steps.title: Condition 1: gender = 'F'
steps.body: Rows with gender F: rollNum 2 (Aliya, 70), 3 (Aliya, 80), 5 (Swati, 65). Rows 1 and 4 (M) are rejected.

steps.title: Condition 2: marks > 65 (strict)
steps.body: Among the F rows: $70>65$ ✓, $80>65$ ✓, $65>65$ ✗ (equal is not greater). Swati's row is rejected.

steps.title: Count the result
steps.body: Rows 2 and 3 satisfy both conditions. They have the same name, but they are different tuples (different rollNum) and there is no DISTINCT anyway, so both are returned: **2 rows**.

cse-2023-cs-51.shortcut: Scan for F rows with marks strictly above 65: 70 and 80 → 2.
pitfalls: Reading $>$ as $\ge$ and including Swati (65): gives 3.
Treating the two "Aliya" rows as duplicates: SELECT * returns both (and they differ in rollNum and marks).

cse-2023-cs-52.approach: A primary index is sparse: one entry (block-anchor key + block pointer) per **data block**. Compute data blocks, index entries per block, index blocks, then the binary-search cost $\lceil\log_2 b\rceil$ on the index — that alone identifies the data block.
cse-2023-cs-52.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| records | 25,000 × 100 B |
| key | 15 B |
| block | 1024 B |
| block pointer | 5 B |

steps.title: Data file: blocking factor and blocks
steps.body:
Records are not split across blocks, so

$$\text{bfr}=\left\lfloor\frac{1024}{100}\right\rfloor=10\ \text{records/block},\qquad \frac{25000}{10}=2500\ \text{data blocks}.$$

steps.title: Index entry size and index blocking factor
steps.body:
Entry $=$ key $+$ pointer $=15+5=20$ B.

$$\text{bfr}_i=\left\lfloor\frac{1024}{20}\right\rfloor=\lfloor51.2\rfloor=51\ \text{entries/block}.$$

steps.title: Number of index blocks
steps.body:
One entry per data block (block anchor) → $2500$ entries.

$$b=\left\lceil\frac{2500}{51}\right\rceil=\lceil49.02\rceil=50\ \text{index blocks}\quad(51\times49=2499<2500).$$

steps.title: Binary search on the index
steps.body:
$$\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6\qquad(2^5=32<50\le64=2^6).$$

The question asks for the accesses needed to **identify** the data block, so the final read of the data block itself is not added: **6**.

cse-2023-cs-52.shortcut: $2500$ data blocks $/\ 51$ entries per index block $\approx50$ index blocks → $\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6$.
pitfalls: Indexing every record (dense): $\lceil25000/51\rceil=491$ blocks → 9. A primary index on an ordered file has one entry per block.
Adding 1 for reading the data block: that gives 7, but the question stops at *identifying* the block.
Using $1024/20=51.2$ without flooring, or $1000/20=50$ with a decimal KB.
cse-2023-cs-52.verification: Sanity: 50 index blocks hold up to $50\times51=2550\ge2500$ entries, and 49 blocks hold only $2499$; binary search over 50 items needs 6 probes ($\lceil\log_2 50\rceil$) since 5 probes cover only 32.

cse-2023-cs-53.approach: Remember only what matters for the future: the number of 1s at the end of the input read so far (0, 1 or 2), plus a trap state once 111 has appeared. Then prove the 4 states are pairwise distinguishable.

steps.title: What the DFA must remember
steps.body:
- $q_0$: the input so far ends in 0 (or is empty) — 0 trailing 1s.
- $q_1$: ends in exactly one 1.
- $q_2$: ends in exactly two 1s.
- dead: "111" has already occurred (the string can never be accepted again).

$q_0,q_1,q_2$ are accepting; dead is not.

steps.title: Transitions
steps.body:
A 0 resets the run of 1s: $q_0,q_1,q_2\xrightarrow{0}q_0$.

A 1 extends it: $q_0\xrightarrow{1}q_1\xrightarrow{1}q_2\xrightarrow{1}\text{dead}$, and dead loops on 0 and 1.

steps.title: Run on 110111: a 0 resets the count
steps.body: $q_0\xrightarrow{1}q_1\xrightarrow{1}q_2\xrightarrow{0}q_0$ — after "110" we are back to 0 trailing 1s.

steps.title: Three consecutive 1s reach the dead state
steps.body: $q_0\xrightarrow{1}q_1\xrightarrow{1}q_2\xrightarrow{1}\text{dead}$: "110111" contains 111 and is rejected — correct.

steps.title: No two states can be merged
steps.body:
Give a string that one state accepts and the other rejects:

| Pair | Distinguishing string |
|---|---|
| any accepting state vs dead | $\varepsilon$ |
| $q_0$ vs $q_1$ | $11$ ($q_0\to q_2$ ✓, $q_1\to$ dead ✗) |
| $q_0$ vs $q_2$ | $1$ |
| $q_1$ vs $q_2$ | $1$ |

All 4 states are pairwise distinguishable, so the minimal (complete) DFA has **4** states.

cse-2023-cs-53.shortcut: "No $k$ consecutive 1s" needs $k$ accepting states (trailing-ones count $0\dots k-1$) plus one dead state: $k+1=4$ for $k=3$.
pitfalls: Answering 3 by dropping the dead state — a DFA's transition function must be total, so the trap state counts.
Building a "contains 111" DFA and forgetting to complement the accepting states.
cse-2023-cs-53.verification: Myhill–Nerode classes: $\varepsilon$, $1$, $11$, $111$ have pairwise distinct futures (as in the table), so at least 4 states are needed; the DFA above has exactly 4.

cse-2023-cs-54.approach: Index bits + offset bits $=\log_2(\text{sets}\times\text{block size})=\log_2(\text{cache size}/\text{associativity})$, so the block size (not given) cancels: tag $=32-\log_2(64\text{ KB}/8)$.
cse-2023-cs-54.given: 8-way, 64 KB $=2^{16}$ B, 32-bit address; block size $B$ not given.

steps.title: Relate sets and block size
steps.body: $$\text{sets}\times\text{ways}\times B=\text{cache size}\;\Rightarrow\;\text{sets}\times B=\frac{2^{16}}{2^3}=2^{13}.$$

steps.title: INDEX + OFFSET bits are fixed
steps.body: $\text{INDEX}+\text{OFFSET}=\log_2(\text{sets})+\log_2 B=\log_2(\text{sets}\times B)=\log_2 2^{13}=13$ bits — whatever $B$ is.

pitfalls: Thinking the block size is needed — it only shifts bits between INDEX and OFFSET.
Using $\log_2(64\text{ KB})=16$ (direct-mapped thinking) → tag 16. Associativity 8 removes 3 index bits and adds them to the tag.
cse-2023-cs-54.verification: Try $B=32$ B: offset 5, sets $=2^{16}/(32\times8)=256$ → index 8; tag $=32-8-5=19$ again.

cse-2023-cs-55.approach: AND the destination with every mask, keep the entries whose result equals the subnet number, and forward on the **longest** matching prefix. Only the octet where the mask is partial needs binary work.

steps.title: Rule: longest matching prefix wins
steps.body: Several entries (and always the default) can match; the router chooses the matching entry with the most 1-bits in its mask. Masks: $255.255.0.0=/16$, $255.255.224.0=/19$, $255.255.255.0=/24$, $255.255.255.224=/27$.

steps.title: Pick the longest match
steps.body: Matching prefixes: /16 (1), /19 (2), /24 (3), default /0 (0). The longest is **/24**, so the packet leaves on **interface 3**.

cse-2023-cs-55.shortcut: Check the most specific entry first: .64/27 covers .64–.95, and 118 is outside; next is 200.150.68.0/24, which contains .118 → interface 3.
pitfalls: Choosing interface 4 because 200.150.68.64 "looks closest" — a /27 covers only 32 addresses (.64–.95).
Taking the first matching row (interface 1) instead of the longest prefix.
cse-2023-cs-55.verification: Range check: /24 entry covers $200.150.68.0$–$.255$ ∋ $.118$; /27 entry covers $.64$–$.95$ ∌ $.118$. So among matches the /24 is the most specific.
